Project_Name: Clam Bayou Mangrove, SAV, and Oyster Restoration Project
Project_Description: Clam Bayou is a shallow, mangrove-lined lagoon located on Sanibel Island, FL, and is adjacent to one of the most visited natural mangrove areas in the country, providing highly visible efforts and outreach opportunities. Degradation of Clam Bayou habitats served as the impetus for the mangrove, seagrass, and shellfish restoration activities which restored nearly 1.5 acres of estuarine fisheries habitat. These efforts included planting of red mangrove propagules and seagrasses, oyster reef construction using bagged oyster shell, and monitoring.
Species_Benefited: (Drum, red), (Manatee, west indian - Range-wide - Endangered), (Oyster, eastern), (Seatrout, spotted), (Snook)

Project_Description: Through a cooperative approach of multiple partners such as the J.N 'Ding' Darling National Wildlife Refuge, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the South Florida Water Management District, and local homeowner's associations, the NOAA Community-based Restoration Program awarded $100,000 in funding to restore tidal flushing between Clam Bayou and Dinkins Bayou, Florida. When developers connected Sanibel and Captiva Islands to the mainland more than 150 acres of mangroves were lost, oyster reefs and seagrass disappeared, water quality declined and important nursery and habitat was severely degraded. Volunteer mangrove planting events were held and more than 2,500 red and black mangroves were planted along the shoreline of Clam Bayou.

Project_Name: Restoring Mangrove Islands in Pine Island Sound
Project_Description: This project restored mangrove and oyster reef habitat for fish and wildlife Species of Greatest Conservation Need in Pine Island Sound using methods demonstrated to work effectively in the area. Pine Island Sound is characterized by extensive mangrove shorelines and mangrove islands, fringing oyster reefs, and shallow seagrass beds which serve as important feeding, breeding, and nursery habitats for fish and wildlife. Repeated hurricanes and sea level rise damaged and degraded habitats on and surrounding five islands managed by the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as part of the Pine Island National Wildlife Refuge: Hemp Key, Bird Key, Benedict Key, Rat Key, and Cat Key. Restoration of resiliency and habitat function at these five islands is being achieved through planting of mangrove propagules, enhancement of oyster reefs, and structural and functional monitoring during this three-year project. Hemp Key is designated by FWC as a Critical Wildlife  Area because it supports a high density of nesting wading and diving birds. Pilot mangrove planting, oyster reef restoration, and initial monitoring were completed by Sanibel- Captiva Conservation Foundation (SCCF) staff and volunteers supported by a State Wildlife Grant (SWG) through USFWS. AHCR provided appropriation funding that was used deliver and stage 50 cubic yards of large fossil shell that was used in oyster reef enhancement. During subsequent grant years SCCF will continue mangrove and oyster restoration and monitoring.
Funding_Program: US Fish and Wildlife Service State Wildlife Grant Program (USFWS SWG)

Project_Name: Jewell Cove Shoreline Restoration (Palm Beach County)
Project_Description: Jewell Cove is an 11.44 acre area that lies within the City of Lake Worth along the eastern shoreline of the Lake Worth Lagoon. The project area included an eroding shoreline, a maritime hammock dominated by exotics, and submerged lands. The purpose of this project was to remove exotic vegetation, protect the shoreline from erosion, and install native plants along 1,100 linear feet of shoreline. Limestone boulders, proven to be viable oyster reef habitat in this area, were installed to protect the shoreline and provide mangrove, Spartina, and oyster habitats. The boulders also add shoreline resilience in regards to climate change and sea level rise and enhance recreational fishing opportunities. Future components of the project, a shell rock pedestrian pathway through the hardwood hammock and an informational kiosk, will add public access and educational opportunities. Jewell Cove is part of a bigger project known as Old Bridge Park. Additional components of the Old Bridge Park project to which this funding did not contribute include repairing a failing seawall and installation of a shade shelter and day-use dock for the public for recreation and fishing. Kiosks and signs about the overall project will be installed to provide information to the public about the environmental benefits and the sponsors of the project. The Old Bridge Park project received additional funding from the Florida Inland Navigation District and from the FDEP through the 2014- 2015 General Appropriations Act program grant. The funding provided by MEHRMA for the Jewell Cove Shoreline portion of the project was used as match towards the FIND and FDEP grants for the Old Bridge Park project. When Old Bridge Park is complete, the total project costs (Old Bridge Park components and Jewell Cove components) are estimated to be approximately $764,000.
Partners: FDEP, Palm Beach County Department of Environmental Resources Management

Project_Description:
The Lake Worth Lagoon estuary in Palm Beach County (PBC) runs approximately 20 miles parallel to the southeast coastline of Florida. It is an urban estuary that has suffered extensive loss of estuarine habitats and degraded water quality due to human development activities over the past century. Approximately 81% of the lagoon’s shoreline is developed with seawalls associated with private residences and businesses. Dredge activities associated with development decades ago resulted in large benthic “holes” that now impair the Lagoon’s ecosystem. These “dredge holes” are typically well below grade, often anoxic, and generally do not support seagrass or wildlife. Additionally, canals that drain into the Lagoon have introduced fine, silty sediments that settle in these holes, hindering recruitment of seagrasses and diminishing water quality. The Tarpon Cove project will expand restoration efforts by filling in a deep dredge hole to restore and enhance important shallow estuarine seagrass habitat through the capping of anoxic, fine-grained organic sediments (i.e., muck). Capping the muck, by filling the hole, will allow for the natural recruitment of seagrasses, including Johnson’s seagrass (Halophila johnsonii), a federally threatened species, to naturally recruit. Additionally, the project will result in five intertidal islands consisting of mangrove, tidal saltmarsh, intertidal sand flat, and oyster reef habitats, along with a beach- nesting bird island. These islands are expected to support over 120 species of fish, 39 species of birds, and 14 state and/or federally listed species including West Indian manatee, Johnson’s sea grass, American oystercatcher and least tern. Other benefits of the project include downstream water-quality improvements, improved wildlife- and fisheries oriented recreational opportunities, increased protection of shorelines from coastal storms and flooding, and increased carbon sequestration capabilities, the latter of which contribute to resilience to the effects of climate change.
The final project, including all phases, will ultimately provide almost 40 acres of restored estuarine habitat.
Funding_Program: National Coastal Wetlands Conservation Grant Program (NCWCGP)
Partners: Palm Beach County Department of Environmental Resources Management (PBC ERM), Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), USFWS State Wildlife Grant Program (SWG)

Project_Description: The Lemon Creek Wetland Restoration Project was implemented within the Charlotte Harbor Watershed in Englewood, Florida. The Lemon Bay Conservancy, in partnership with the Southwest Florida Water Management District, restored an abandoned 80-acre golf course now known as Wildflower Preserve. The project plans included improving the tidal connectivity between Lemon Creek and Lemon Bay, enhancing the existing freshwater and estuarine wetlands, adding nine acres of estuarine wetlands, adding five acres of freshwater wetlands, removing exotic vegetation, and adding native wetland and coastal upland plantings. The project was specifically designed to enhance freshwater and oligohaline fisheries, wading and shorebird habitat, and overall ecosystem function within the watershed.
Restoration_Technique: hydrologic restoration, process-based physical restoration, species control, planting

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration - Walton Scrub Preserve (St. Lucie County)
Project_Description:
This entry is one of 10 project sites included under the name "Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration". 

The Indian River Lagoon Council will implement a large-scale restoration in response to an urgent need to restore essential fish habitats, enhance ecosystem functions, and increase resilience in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) on the Atlantic Coast of Florida.  The overall project design integrates a multi-habitat and multi-site restoration approach that recognizes the complex spatial and temporal diversity of the IRL. The overall project includes a network of 10 discrete project sites and 15 individual projects that cumulatively include restoration and/or enhancement of  seagrass (46 acres), oyster (6.5 acres), saltmarsh wetland (2,125 acres), and living shoreline (6,045 linear feet) habitats.  The project will also re-introduce native clams (21 million) to enhance seagrass habitat.  The ten individual projects will engage the community through site specific outreach events and volunteer opportunities.  

This project will restore coastal resilience to an eroded shoreline with failing revetments that pose an immediate threat to South Indian River Drive, an important north-south transportation corridor adjacent to the Walton Scrub Preserve. The restoration of 1.75 acres of shoreline will be achieved by constructing 3 oyster reefs and planting mangroves and smooth cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora).  An acre of seagrass habitat will be enhanced through plantings.

The Indian River Lagoon Council will implement a large-scale restoration in response to an urgent need to restore essential fish habitats, enhance ecosystem functions, and increase resilience in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) on the Atlantic Coast of Florida.  The overall project design integrates a multi-habitat and multi-site restoration approach that recognizes the complex spatial and temporal diversity of the IRL. The overall project includes a network of 10 discrete project sites and 15 individual projects that cumulatively include restoration and/or enhancement of  seagrass (46 acres), oyster (6.5 acres), saltmarsh wetland (2,125 acres), and living shoreline (6,045 linear feet) habitats.  The project will also re-introduce native clams (21 million) to enhance seagrass habitat.  The ten individual projects will engage the community through site specific outreach events and volunteer opportunities.  

This project will restore coastal resilience to an eroded shoreline with failing revetments that pose an immediate threat to South Indian River Drive, an important north-south transportation corridor adjacent to the Walton Scrub Preserve. The restoration of 1.75 acres of shoreline will be achieved by constructing 3 oyster reefs and planting mangroves and smooth cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora).  An acre of seagrass habitat will be enhanced through plantings.

Project_Description: The Florida Institute of Saltwater Heritage (FISH) restored approximately 24.5 acres of mangrove, wetlands, and upland habitat within the FISH Preserve in Manatee County, Florida.  FISH is dedicated to the promotion and preservation of the cultural and environmental integrity of Florida's traditional maritime communities.  In 2000 FISH was able to acquire 95 acres of coastal habitat adjacent to the Village of Cortez and Sarasota Bay and called it the FISH Preserve.  This restoration project restored tidal circulation to the preserve, removed invasive species and planted native vegetation to restore important fish habitat.

Project_Name: FISH Preserve Coastal Resotration and Enhancement Phase III
Project_Description: Florida Institute for Saltwater Heritage (FISH) Preserve is a 100- acre publically-accessible community conservation property in the historic Village of Cortez, Manatee County. The project area includes tidal creek, mangroves, saltmarsh, and coastal hammock habitats. The purpose of this project is to restore tidal wetland function and enhance habitats for estuarine- dependent species. This project builds upon the success of two completed phases of restoration, continuing the planned control of exotic invasive plants, creation of tidal creeks, and planting of intertidal marsh with beneficial native grasses. This project involved engineering and design plan updates during 2018 and 2019, as well as development of specifications for construction. The project is fully shovel- ready for construction of Phase III during fiscal year 2019/2020. Additional project funding in FY18/19 was contributed by Sarasota Bay Estuary Program (SBEP), the project partner and permittee, through in-kind project management services. $284,000 in leveraged funds from the first two phases of the project were provided by SBEP, Southwest Florida Water Management District, and Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership.
Partners: Sarasota Bay Estuary Program (SBEP), Southwest Florida Water Management District (SWFWMD), Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership

Project_Name: GT Bray Stormwater Pond Restoration Planting
Project_Description: G.T. Bray Parkís freshwater pond was restored to help reestablish a healthy ecosystem. Once a natural wetland, the pond was deepened in the 1970s and used to store reclaimed water in the 1980s and 1990s. Over time, it became overgrown with invasive vegetation and saw elevated nutrient levels. Restoration efforts included removing invasive species and planting native wetland and buffer zone vegetation. A major planting in 2024, completed with the Sarasota Bay Estuary Program, was lost during the hurricane season. The project continued with the goal of stabilizing the shoreline, improving water quality, and enhancing wildlife habitat.

Project_Description: This project restored the degraded saltmarsh and mangrove systems of Wildcat Cove Preserve within St. Lucie County, Florida.  This 129-acre site was impounded in the 1960’s for mosquito control purposes.  The Wildcat Cove restoration project reconnected the site to the Indian River Lagoon by removing invasive vegetation and installing six culverts.  This on-the-ground restoration project benefits living marine resources by increasing available habitat that is important to the refuge, spawning, and rearing areas essential to fisheries.  Not only did this project help to stabilize this estuarine system, but it also educated and engaged the local community through native species planting events and educational signage placed throughout the preserve. Approximately 99 acres of saltmarsh and mangrove habitat was restored.

Project_Name: Egmont Key National Wildlife Refuge Vegetation Management and Dune Retention
Project_Description:
This project will restore, protect, and enhance coastal wading bird, seabird, and shorebird nesting and foraging habitat on Egmont Key National Wildlife Refuge (NWR) through the removal of invasive vegetation, planting of native plant species, and subsequent reduction in shoreline erosion.

Specifically, this project will:
•      Remove invasive plants by conducting chemical treatment and mechanical removal of coin vine, with subsequent pile burning, on approximately 12 untreated acres and 12 previously treated acres in areas that were, are, or could potentially be bird-nesting habitat; and
•      Restore and protect bird-nesting habitat by planting native vegetation and installing sand fencing, where appropriate.
Plant_Type: Railroad vine, Beach morning glory, Sea grape

Project_Description: The Ft. DeSoto Monitoring Project implemented pre and post-construction monitoring to capture the effects of re-opening tidal connections that were closed during the 1950s and 1960s in the back bays of Mullet Key.  The historic tidal connections were lost by the construction of a man-made causeway, but were reestablished in 2004 by installing a bridge to restore circuitous tidal flow.  Data from seagrass samples, water quality samples, sediment cores, and temperature loggers, etc. were all collected to document the benefit of this project on the Ft. DeSoto ecosystem.

Project_Description: Through funding from NOAA’s Restoration Center, in partnership with the US Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the Pinellas County Environmental Foundation, and others, volunteers constructed a bridge to restore circulation to the back bays of Mullet Key in Ft. DeSoto Park, Florida. Tidal flow between bays in the Fort DeSoto Park Aquatic Habitat Management Area in Pinellas County were severed during the dredging and filling activities that occurred in the late 1950s.  Summertime temperatures become extremely elevated in these areas leading to very low dissolved oxygen levels as well as severe seagrass stress. Restored circulation has improved water quality healthier essential fish habitat. Fish and crabs had migrated into the area within a few days.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Stewardship Initiative Phase IV
Project_Description: This project, the Tampa Bay Stewardship Initiative, conducted environmental restoration and education through the 'Hands On Tampa Bay', a program of Tampa Bay Watch.   Through a combination of field trips, teacher curriculum workshops, and summer camps this project implemented a variety of activities.  More than 3,000 students and 750 teachers/aides were educated about the importance of and the issues facing the Tampa Bay ecosystem.  Students and campers helped to replant approximately 1 acre of saltmarsh at Ft. De Soto Park and Cunningham Key.  In addition, volunteers and program participants also constructed and installed 75 concrete oyster domes along Bayshore Boulevard in Tampa and more than 200 ft. of oyster bar  along Whale Island in Pinellas County.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration - Bee Gum Point (IR Land Trust)
Project_Description:
This entry is one of 10 project sites included under the name "Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration". 

The Indian River Lagoon Council will implement a large-scale restoration in response to an urgent need to restore essential fish habitats, enhance ecosystem functions, and increase resilience in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) on the Atlantic Coast of Florida.  The overall project design integrates a multi-habitat and multi-site restoration approach that recognizes the complex spatial and temporal diversity of the IRL. The overall project includes a network of 10 discrete project sites and 15 individual projects that cumulatively include restoration and/or enhancement of  seagrass (46 acres), oyster (6.5 acres), saltmarsh wetland (2,125 acres), and living shoreline (6,045 linear feet) habitats.  The project will also re-introduce native clams (21 million) to enhance seagrass habitat.  The ten individual projects will engage the community through site specific outreach events and volunteer opportunities.  

This project in the central IRL will enhance 125 acres of impounded wetlands and 10 acres of seagrass habitat through the installation of two culverts.  The project will also  enhance a living shoreline through mangrove plantings and will deploy Spartan Fish Reefs to enhance essential fish habitat along the shoreline.  Volunteer opportunities will be created through the Indian River Land Trust and fishing opportunities will be improved for local subsistence fishers.

Project_Description: The Jones Pier Conservation Area (JPCA) is part of the rich history of late 19th century/early 20th century settlement in Indian River County. In 1889, Seaborn Jones and his family homesteaded 160 acres on Orchid Island. Mr. Jones and his neighbors built the “Orchid-Narrows Road” which is now known as Jungle Trail (listed in 2003 on the National Register of Historic Places). The 16- acre JPCA that was purchased by the County in 2011 (including the docks) is part of this original homestead. The County acquired the site from the Jones’ family with assistance from the Florida Communities Trust (FCT). As part of the purchase, the County committed to implementing a management plan for the site that restores ecological value, while at the same time utilizes the existing buildings on the property for public access and display of educational and historical exhibits. To this end, the County has developed a Master Plan for the site that includes restoration/creation of wetlands on-site as well as a Living Shoreline. The improvements include the creation of a 2.8-acre high marsh community that will filter Lagoon waters (Fig. 1). High marsh is a rare resource in this portion of the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), and it is anticipated that this wetland will provide diverse habitat and improved water quality in proximity to the site. The construction of the high marsh is to be funded, in part, through a grant from the Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program (IRLNEP) with matching funds from the County. The discharge location for the high marsh wetland occurs within a section of shoreline where concrete and rubble were deposited historically to minimize erosion. There is minimal coverage by desirable shoreline vegetation, and very little potential habitat for wildlife. The entire 2.25-mile section of Jungle Trail that fronts the Lagoon is devoid of emergent herbaceous vegetation. MEHRMA funds provide for the construction of ~125 linear feet of functional living shoreline along Jungle trail, a highly visible section of the Indian River Lagoon. The living shoreline will function as the terminal section of the habitat and water quality improvement efforts on the JPCA. During FY 2018/19, MEHRMA funds were used to purchase the native coquina rock boulders which will be placed along the shoreline and coupled with native plants. The County also plans to incorporate extensive educational displays showcasing the importance of these types of habitats with respect to the ecology of the Lagoon environment.

Project_Description: This project will remove invasive species, primarily Brazilian pepper, and re-create a variety of native estuarine, freshwater, and upland habitats.  The disturbed portion of the site will be re-contoured into productive estuarine habitat by planting roughly 25,000 native plants with volunteers.  At higher elevations, the cleared area will be turned into freshwater ponds. An education signage will be installed when the project is completed to educate the public about the importance of the habitat to fisheries and avifaunal species.  Nearby, and additional component was added which increases mangrove habitat and improves hydrologic connection to saltern areas.

Project_Description: Green Key is a small island located near the mouth of the Alafia River in an area of Tampa Bay, FL commonly referred to as the Kitchen. This project created of a series of oyster bars was in an effort to prevent further erosion, create habitat, improve water quality, and buffer the area from wave action, providing optimal conditions for the settlement of salt marsh plants and mangroves. Five oyster bars were installed on Green Key in two events. In all, 24 tons of fossilized oyster shell was deposited on the shoreline of Green Key. After 24 months, the created reefs have excellent oyster growth and appear to be healthy. Funding was provided through NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program partnership with the Fish America Foundation.

Project_Name: Mulberry Mangrove/Tidal Creek Project and Lewis Lake Project
Project_Description: On December 7, 1997, over 50 million gallons of acidic process water was released into the Alafia River from a fertilizer plant in Mulberry, Polk County, Florida. The release injured natural resources in the Alafia River and in Tampa Bay. Several public agencies, including NOAA, FDEP and EPC, worked together to assess natural resource injuries and losses caused by the Spill and to recover natural resource damages to compensate for these losses from the party responsible. This project consisted of two components implemented on MacDill Airforce Base: the Mangrove/Tidal Creek project and the Lewis Lake Project.  The first component involved the restoration of 34 acres of intertidal lagoons/channels, high and low marsh platforms, mangrove islands, upland islands, upland hammocks, and relic mangrove forest. To accomplish project goals, large stands of non-native vegetation had to be removed, followed by excavation of lagoons and channels to restore tidal availability. The second component, the Lewis Lake Project, modified an existing freshwater/oligohaline stormwater treatment pond that was intermittently intertidal via the pond’s overflow control structure. This 26.6 acre project increased the size of the pond, created new open water and marsh platforms, removed all cattails and other nuisance/non-native plants from marsh platforms, and resulted in improved water quality for the bay due to enhanced stormwater treatment capacity of the pond.
Restoration_Technique: process-based physical restoration, species control, planting
Lead_Implementer: Southwest Florida Water Management District-S.W.I.M. Program

The release injured natural resources in the Alafia River and in Tampa Bay. Several public agencies, including NOAA, FDEP and EPC, worked together to assess natural resource injuries and losses caused by the Spill and to recover natural resource damages to compensate for these losses from the party responsible. This project consisted of two components implemented on MacDill Airforce Base: the Mangrove/Tidal Creek project and the Lewis Lake Project.  The first component involved the restoration of 34 acres of intertidal lagoons/channels, high and low marsh platforms, mangrove islands, upland islands, upland hammocks, and relic mangrove forest. To accomplish project goals, large stands of non-native vegetation had to be removed, followed by excavation of lagoons and channels to restore tidal availability. The second component, the Lewis Lake Project, modified an existing freshwater/oligohaline stormwater treatment pond that was intermittently intertidal via the pond’s overflow control structure. This 26.6 acre project increased the size of the pond, created new open water and marsh platforms, removed all cattails and other nuisance/non-native plants from marsh platforms, and resulted in improved water quality for the bay due to enhanced stormwater treatment capacity of the pond.
Restoration_Technique: process-based physical restoration, species control, planting
Lead_Implementer: Southwest Florida Water Management District-S.W.I.M. Program

Project_Description: In order to restore 200 yards of native shoreline per year near the Ballast Point Park on Hillsborough Bay, non-profit restoration group Tampa Bay Watch and the Coastal Conservation Association of Tampa were awarded grants through partnerships between NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and Fish America Foundation and Restore America's Estuaries. Oyster domes were used to provide oyster settlement and structure for small fish. Several events were held for volunteers to build the necessary number of domes for the project. Project_Name: Recording Manatee Movements in Tampa Bay
Project_Description: Research using state-of-the-art GPS equipment and data loggers (Argos-linked GPS and time-depth-temperature data loggers) was coupled with an ongoing project entitled, "Calibrating Manatee Aerial Survey Counts at Tampa Bay Power Plants in Winter."   The primary objective of this study was to obtain detailed information on manatee movements around Tampa Bay power plants that allows researchers and natural resource managers to understand how manatees are using these warm-water sites.  Identification of these important habitats is critical to the long term protection and conservation of manatees and their habitats.
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

Project_Description: This restoration project helped to stabilize the shoreline and restore fisheries habitat at the Richard T. Paul Alafia Bank Bird Sanctuary in eastern Hillsborough Bay in Tampa, Florida. This island has been eroding over the years due to large boat wakes caused by ship traffic in this stretch of Tampa Bay.  This project installed a series of pyramid shaped wave attenuation devices along 250 ft. of shoreline to reduce erosion and stabilize the habitat behind this installed reef.  This project helped to leverage more than 650 ft. of additional shoreline restoration along the Bird Sanctuary.  In addition, the area behind the wave attenuation devices was planted with saltmarsh species to help jumpstart natural recruitment.
Restoration_Technique: process-based physical restoration, erosion control, reef construction, planting
Lead_Implementer: Florida Coastal Islands Sanctuaries - Audubon of Florida

Project_Name: Fantasy Island Salt Marsh and Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: The Coastal Conservation Association of Florida has partnered with Tampa Bay Watch, the Florida Aquarium, and local Boy Scout troops to create a series of new oyster bars at Fantasy Island and Green Key. The oyster reef will help prevent shoreline erosion, provide hard bottom habitat, and improve water quality in the Tampa Bay estuary. In addition, 40 sixth graders, their parents, teachers and volunteers planted 5,000 plugs of salt marsh grasses along one acre of shoreline. A second planting added 2,000 plugs of smooth cordgrass. NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and the Fish America Foundation provided partial funding to support this project.

Project_Description: The Mayor's Beautification Program conducted Phase II of the 'Tampa Shoreline Restoration Initiative', a community-based project that supported habitat restoration projects across 6 sites within the City of Tampa.  This project completed the Shoreline Tracking and Reporting System, as well as the Tampa Shoreline Restoration Initiative Master Plan.  Both tools will be instrumental in future restoration design and planning for the City of Tampa.  More than 2,000 volunteers participated in close to 80 individual conservation and restoration projects during this project.  In total more than 12,000 native plants were installed and approximately 6.5 acres of coastal habitat were restored.

Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch in partnership with the Coastal Conservation Association of Florida and local community groups created a series of new oyster bars and planted salt marsh habitat at A.J. Palonis Jr. Park in Tampa Bay. Oyster shell material was placed on the tidal flats to create oyster reefs at five sites within the park and salt marsh vegetation was planted on the shoreline behind the new oyster reefs in an effort to restore lost habitat, prevent further erosion of shorelines and improve water quality through natural filtration. A total of 153 volunteers contributed 624 hours to place nearly 40 tons of shell in the restoration site. Funding for this project was provided by the NOAA Restoration Center's Community-based Restoration Program and Fish America Foundation.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration - Satellite Beach (FWC)
Project_Description:
This entry is one of 10 project sites included under the name "Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration". 

The Indian River Lagoon Council will implement a large-scale restoration in response to an urgent need to restore essential fish habitats, enhance ecosystem functions, and increase resilience in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) on the Atlantic Coast of Florida.  The overall project design integrates a multi-habitat and multi-site restoration approach that recognizes the complex spatial and temporal diversity of the IRL. The overall project includes a network of 10 discrete project sites and 15 individual projects that cumulatively include restoration and/or enhancement of  seagrass (46 acres), oyster (6.5 acres), saltmarsh wetland (2,125 acres), and living shoreline (6,045 linear feet) habitats.  The project will also re-introduce native clams (21 million) to enhance seagrass habitat.  The ten individual projects will engage the community through site specific outreach events and volunteer opportunities.  

The Samson Island project in the Banana River, part of the Indian River Lagoon Estuary, is a large scale seagrass and living shoreline project that aims to restore 10 acres of mixed seagrass species and stabilizing 700 linear feet of shoreline. These goals will be achieved by planing 15,000 seagrass planting units and 1,200 mangroves (shoreline).  Wave attenuation devices will also be implemented to reduce energy to aid seagrass recovery.

These goals will be achieved by planing 15,000 seagrass planting units and 1,200 mangroves (shoreline).  Wave attenuation devices will also be implemented to reduce energy to aid seagrass recovery.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Impoundment Reconnection and Restoration
Project_Description: The St. John River Water Management District worked with the Brevard County Mosquito Control District and the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to install culverts to enhance fish habitat in Brevard County, FL.  At the Sykes Creek Impoundments (C-2 North and C-2 South), which comprise nearly 2,015 acres of wetland, 17 culverts were installed to recreate flow where natural creek mouths previously existed and provide fish with access to habitat.  Work began on this component in September of 2015, restoring 1,289 acres.  The balance of acreage was completed in the fall of 2015.  Additional work is being implemented in other impoundments within the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to address subsidence. Subsidence has reduced sediment levels to elevations too low to support marsh grass or mangrove habitat.  This component of the project was implemented first as a pilot project to evaluate a variety of methods to bring subsided areas up to an appropriate elevation to support vegetation typical of wetlands in the area.  The pilot effort was completed in the spring of 2016.  Project results will lead to implementation of an expanded effort in the fall of 2016/winter of 2017.

Project_Name: Port Orange Living Shoreline and Oyster Reef
Project_Description: This effort was the first pilot project implemented as part of the larger Port Orange Shoreline Management Plan.  This project implemented a combination of living shoreline restoration techniques in a highly urbanized system to demonstrate the different shoreline stabilization techniques available for use in lieu of more traditional hardened shorelines.  With the permission of 16 homeowners the project was able to restore 0.5 acres of shoreline habitat composed of upland, saltmarsh, and oyster reef habitat. With the help of the project partners and 279 volunteers invasive species were removed, upland habitats were stabilized, Spartina was planted, and a variety of oyster restoration techniques were deployed.  Lessons learned from this project will be incorporated into future restoration efforts associated with the Port Orange Shoreline Management Plan.

Project_Name: North Peninsula State Park Saltmarsh Restoration- Phase 2
Project_Description: This project removes spoil sediment placed during the dredging of the Intracoastal Waterway, to re-establish estuarine wetlands on the site.  Through the removal of invasive species and grading of the site, the project will provide nursery habitat benefits to a variety of commercially and recreationally important fisheries species.  This project will restore the final 20 acres of the 95 acres of spoil-filled marsh that have been identified for restoration within the North Peninsula State Park.  As of September 2015, the southern 10 acres of the site have been cleared, graded and planted.  A volunteer planting event was held on September 12th to celebrate this accomplishment.  The work will continue into the fall until the site is complete.

Combining these objectives, this project created breakwaters to reduce wave energy, increased benthic secondary productivity, and created salt marsh habitat. Project_Name: Invasive Plant Removal at Gulf Islands National Seashore
Project_Description: This project originally intended to aggressively treat the five most problematic invasive plant species in the Fort Pickens, Santa Rosa, and Perdido Key areas of Gulf Islands National Seashore (GUIS). However, when the original survey of the project area occurred, ALL invasive plant species found were identified and inventoried and are being treated under this project -- that total currently being 23 species. The project is helping to gradually restore coastal habitats and native plant species in these areas, which will likely allow native animal populations that depend on these coastal habitats and plants to also improve. The project will last for approximately six years. Activities include: 1) locating and mapping the invasive species; 2) evaluating past and current treatment methods, researching new treatment methods, and developing a Treatment Action Plan (TAP) (this ended up being titled "Invasive Managment Plan"); 3) treating these species in accordance with the Plan for five years and reducing their populations to sizes that can be more easily managed by park staff in the future; both chemical and mechanical treatment methods are being used, as appropriate; 4) monitoring treatment success regularly to determine the treatment plan for the following year; 5) preparing a Project Completion Report that describes the work done and includes recommendations for future treatments; and 6) using information gathered and knowledge gained to provide the basis for an Exotic Plant Management Plan for GUIS (this was prepared in 2021 and titled "Invasive Management Plan"). The entire project area was surveyed for invasive plants in 2020 and every year since. Treatments and removal started in 2021 and have occurred every year since. Torpedo grass dominates as the most widespread invasive plant and is being treated by a contractor.

Project_Name: Norriego Point Restoration and Recreation Project
Project_Description: This project involves stabilizing, enhancing and re-establishing recreational activities available at Norriego Point. The restoration work involves the construction of several erosion control structures to dissipate wave energy and protect the dredged fill placed landward of the revetment. Two new embayments will provide additional swimming areas as well as more space for boats and kayaks to pull in. Additionally, facilities will include a harborside boardwalk, dune crossovers, a picnic pavilion with restrooms, showers, and drinking fountains; educational signage to encourage appreciation of this natural environment; a multi-use trail, bike racks, and vehicle parking along the access road adjacent to the park land.

Project_Name: Green Shores Oyster Reef and Saltmarsh Creation
Project_Description: NOAA’s Community-Based Restoration Program partnered with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, the United States Navy, Fish America Foundation, the Nature Conservancy, and others to construct an oyster reef breakwater from limestone rock and oyster shell and create an intertidal salt marsh area behind the reef in a 15 acre area of Pensacola Bay. The restoration site is already highly productive, hosting up to 800 birds a day as well as many marine fish and invertebrates.

Project_Description: Goffinsville Park is a popular park managed by Nassau County, within the Nassau River – St. Johns River Marshes Aquatic Preserve. The Park includes a playground, picnic area, restrooms, fishing pier, and public boat ramp. A living shoreline was completed in 2016 along approximately 200’ of shoreline on the western edge of the park. This project built on the success of the 2016 efforts by installing multiple non-plastic oyster restoration materials to serve as a wave break in front of the seawall, extending the existing living shoreline. This arrangement allows for side-by-side comparison of multiple oyster restoration materials, including CORE modules, Reefballs, and Reef Prisms. The project is intended to enhance estuarine habitat, improve water quality, and reduce erosion while engaging the public. Volunteers and citizen scientists were involved in the project via the Florida Master Naturalist Program, IFAS Extension opportunities, and the Florida Master Gardener Program. The Park now serves as a demonstration site for homeowners to physically view available material options when planning to install a living shoreline along their own waterfront property. High-quality educational signs displayed above the demonstration area outline the benefits of living shorelines and the specific materials utilized at the site.
